title: Learning Dynamic Causal Graphs Under Parametric Uncertainty via Polynomial Chaos Expansions
claim: Raw time-series data flows through staged discovery, refinement and uncertainty quantification to yield an interpretable, parameter-dependent causal graph.
layout: 4 panels, left-to-right, bold arrows between dashed-border stages
description: A four-stage left-to-right pipeline with bold black arrows between dashed rounded boxes, each topped by a colored title banner. The first box, Industrial Data in green, shows bar and line time-series plots above stacked cards for four time steps (t=k-3 to t=k). The cards hold temperature, pressure, flow and concentration values, and the last card is highlighted in blue. The second box has a pink Skeleton Discovery banner over an undirected network. Below it, an orange Edge Refinement banner sits under a DAG adjacency matrix and a directed graph with colored nodes. The third box is a yellow Uncertainty Quantification stage. It has a plot of trajectories with confidence bands, an edge-frequency histogram in cyan, and Bootstrap and Sobol Sensitivity buttons. The final box is a blue Discovered Dynamic Causal Graph with nodes X1 to X9, colored arrows, and small annotation boxes giving effect sizes and confidence intervals.
caption: Overview of the polynomial chaos theory for causal discovery framework in dynamic uncertainty systems.
abstract: Existing causal discovery methods are fundamentally limited by the assumption of a static causal graph, a constraint that fails in real-world systems where causal relationships dynamically vary with underlying system parameters. This discrepancy prevents the application of causal discovery in critical domains such as industrial process control, where understanding how causal effects change is essential. We address this gap by proposing a new paradigm that moves beyond static graphs to learn functional causal representations. We introduce a framework that models each causal link not as a static weight but as a function of measurable system parameters. By representing these functions using Polynomial Chaos Expansions (PCE), we develop a tractable method to learn the complete parametric causal structure from observational data. We provide theoretical proofs for the identifiability of these functional models and introduce a novel, provably convergent learning algorithm. On a large-scale chemical reactor dataset, our method learns the dynamic causal structure with a 90.9% F1-score, nearly doubling the performance of state-of-the-art baselines and providing an interpretable model of how causal mechanisms evolve.
